---
title: "Question 1 Initial Analysis"
---

# Notable Results:
- When comparing the differences in people interested in software development and those that are not interested, the people interested in software development seemed to have a higher proportion of interest in software integration, image analysis, data engineering, and neural networks compared to those who did not express interest in software development (at least 20 percentage points more!)

- The respondents interested in neuroscience were also more interested in image analysis compared to those not interested in neuroscience (38 percentage points more). Similar behavior was seen between those interested in health/biology compared to those who weren't interested. (Makes sense since imaging can be a significant part of those fields)

- Respondents interested in biology seemed to express less interest in statistical modeling compared to those not interested in biology. (32 percentage points lower) I don't have an explanation for this.

- The proportion of respondents interested in time series is 27 percentage points higher among those interested in environmental science compared to those that are not. (Maybe environmental science likes to look at long term trends which includes time series data)

- The proportion of respondents interested in statistical modeling is 31 percentage points higher in respondents interested in social and political science compared to those who are not. (Potentially may be because social and political science may use a lot of models to predict behavior or stuff like elections). Similar behavior was seen for predictive modeling and time series.

```{r Load in Packages and Data}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
interest <- read_csv("../data/interest-clean.csv")
```
Question of interest: Is there a relation between people's domains of interest (like biology, technology, AI, etc.) and the areas of data science that they prefer?

# 8 Domains of Interest + Other 
- Environmental Science
- Social or Political Science
- Ecology
- Biology
- Public health
- Neuroscience
- Technology
- Software Development
- Other

# 11 Areas of Data Science + Other
- Analysis or classification of images
- Deep learning and neural networks
- Spatial statistics or time series analysis 
- Data acquisition and engineering
- Natural language processing and analysis of text
- Model deployment and software or web integrations
- Data visualization and interactive dashboards
- Predictive modeling, generally
- Statistical models and inference, generally
- Databases
- Algorithms
- Other

```{r}
# Function to help classify whether a certain domain was selected. 
# Currently does not handle written-in values for the "Other" option

add_domains <- function(data){
  data %>% mutate(envi_sci = grepl("Environmental Science", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  soc_poli_sci = grepl("Social or Political Science", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  ecology = grepl("Ecology", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  biology = grepl("Biology", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  health = grepl("Public health", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  neurosci = grepl("Neuroscience", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  tech = grepl("Technology", domains, ignore.case = T),
                  software_dev = grepl("Software Development", domains, ignore.case = T)
                  )
}

add_areas <- function(data){
  data %>% mutate(image_analysis = grepl("Analysis or classification of images", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  neural_networks = grepl("Deep learning and neural networks", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  time_series = grepl("Spatial statistics or time series analysis", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  data_engineering = grepl("Data acquisition and engineering", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  text_analysis = grepl("Natural language processing and analysis of text", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  software_integration = grepl("Model deployment and software or web integrations", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  data_visualization = grepl("Data visualization and interactive dashboards", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  predictive_modeling = grepl("Predictive modeling, generally", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  statistical_modeling = grepl("Statistical models and inference, generally", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  databases = grepl("Databases", areas, ignore.case = T),
                  algorithms = grepl("Algorithms", areas, ignore.case = T)
                  )
}

# Clean up the data. Add a column for each area/domain.
interest <- interest %>% add_domains() %>% add_areas() %>% select(-c("type", "language"))
```

```{r Aggregating Results}
# Quick look at the proportion of respondents selecting each domain or each data science area. 
domains_of_interest <- interest %>% select(envi_sci:software_dev) %>% colSums() %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column() 
colnames(domains_of_interest) <- c("domain", "count")
domains_of_interest <- domains_of_interest %>% mutate(prop = count / 49)

areas_of_interest <- interest %>% select(image_analysis:algorithms) %>% colSums() %>% as.data.frame() %>% rownames_to_column() 
colnames(areas_of_interest) <- c("area", "count")
areas_of_interest <- areas_of_interest %>% mutate(prop = count / 49)
```



```{r Preliminary Plots}
# Proportion of Respondents that chose a domain
ggplot(domains_of_interest , aes(x = domain, y = prop)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,1)) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Proportion", title = "Proportion of Respondents Specifying a Domain is of Interest to Them")

# Proportion of Respondents that chose an area of data science
# X-Axis with Data Science Area names are hard to read because they overlap.
ggplot(areas_of_interest , aes(x = area, y = prop)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,1)) +
  labs(x = "Area", y = "Proportion", title = "Proportion of Respondents Specifying an Area of Data Science is of Interest to Them")

areas_of_interest %>% arrange(prop %>% desc())
```

```{r Creating a 2 way frequency table}
# Creates a frequency table showing all the paired selections between domains and areas
# Note the count table margins add up to big numbers since students can select multiple areas and multiple domains. That is, a single student can be represented multiple times.
all_domains <- interest %>% select("envi_sci":"software_dev") %>% colnames()
all_areas <- interest %>% select("image_analysis":"algorithms") %>% colnames()
domain_area_count_table <- matrix(nrow = 8, ncol = 11)
colnames(domain_area_count_table) <- all_areas
rownames(domain_area_count_table) <- all_domains

for(domain in all_domains){
  counts = interest %>% filter(.data[[domain]] == T) %>% select(any_of(all_areas)) %>% colSums()
  domain_area_count_table[match(domain, all_domains),] <- counts
}
domain_area_count_table %>% as.data.frame()
```


```{r Creating a 2 way proportion table}
# Same thing, but with a proportion table. The proportions are calculated with the denominator being the number of people who selected the domain.
# For example: 5 people selected ecology. Then each proportion in the ecology column is calculated with the number of people who selected the area divided by 5.
domain_area_prop_table <- matrix(nrow = 8, ncol = 11)
colnames(domain_area_prop_table) <- all_areas
rownames(domain_area_prop_table) <- all_domains

for(domain in all_domains){
  counts = interest %>% filter(.data[[domain]] == T) %>% select(any_of(all_areas)) %>% colMeans()
  domain_area_prop_table[match(domain, all_domains),] <- counts
}

long_prop_table <- domain_area_prop_table %>% as.table() %>% as.data.frame()
colnames(long_prop_table) <- c("Domain", "Area", "Proportion")
long_prop_table$Domain <-  factor(long_prop_table$Domain, levels = domains_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(domain))
long_prop_table$Area <- factor(long_prop_table$Area, levels = areas_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(area))

area_int_strat_domain_plot <- ggplot(long_prop_table, aes(x = Domain, y = Area, fill = Proportion)) + geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = round(Proportion, 2)), col = "white") + labs(title = "Proportion of Interest within a Data Science Area Stratified by Domain", subtitle = "Selection frequency increases left to right, bottom to top") + theme(text = element_text(size = 9))
```
If there is no relation between a person's domain of interest and the areas of data science they are interested in, we would expect each column to look about the same.

```{r}
# What might be more useful is if you compare proportions as a deviation from the average.
prop_deviations <- inner_join(long_prop_table %>% rename(area = Area), areas_of_interest, by = "area") %>% transmute(Domain, area, prop_dev = Proportion - prop)
prop_deviations$Domain <- factor(prop_deviations$Domain, levels = domains_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(domain))
prop_deviations$area <- factor(prop_deviations$area, levels = areas_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(area))

ggplot(prop_deviations, aes(x = Domain, y = area, fill = prop_dev)) + 
  geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = round(prop_dev, 2)), col = "white") + labs(title = "Proportion Deviation Stratified by Domain",  subtitle = "Selection frequency increases left to right, bottom to top")
domains_of_interest %>% arrange(count)
```
One issue with interpreting this heatmap is that the proportion of people choosing each domain varies. Specifically for tech, 45/49 people chose that as a domain of interest, so the deviation from the overall survey data won't be significant since the tech strata already contains most of the data. This is more useful for the other domains where they make up 40-53% of the results. (Software dev makes up 69%). Ecology has a very small group of 5 people only, so its values may be extra big because each response would swing a proportion by 20%.

```{r}
# Bar plot for interest in a domain
ggplot(domains_of_interest , aes(x = domain, y = prop)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,1)) +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Proportion", title = "Proportion of Respondents Specifying a Domain is of Interest to Them")

domains_of_interest # Frequencies and proportions of each domain

# Bar plot for interest in a data science area (labels are overlapping, so not very helpful)
ggplot(areas_of_interest , aes(x = area, y = prop)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0,1)) +
  labs(x = "Area", y = "Proportion", title = "Proportion of Respondents Specifying an Area of Data Science is of Interest to Them")

areas_of_interest # Frequencies and proportions of each area

domain_area_count_table %>% as.data.frame() # contingency table of domains and data science areas

# Two-way proportion table stratified by domain
ggplot(long_prop_table, aes(x = Domain, y = Area, fill = Proportion)) + geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = round(Proportion, 2)), col = "white") + labs(title = "Proportion of Each Data Science Area Selected Stratified by Domain", subtitle = "Selection frequency increases left to right, bottom to top")

# Two-way proportion deviation table stratified by domain. Each value is the domain-stratified proportion's deviation from the overall survey data proportion. 
ggplot(prop_deviations, aes(x = Domain, y = area, fill = prop_dev)) + 
  geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = round(prop_dev, 2)), col = "white") + labs(title = "Proportion Deviation Stratified by Domain",  subtitle = "Selection frequency increases left to right, bottom to top")
``` 

# Takeaways
- I'm looking at the "Proportion Deviation Stratified by Domain" heatmap. Ignoring tech (because it makes up 90% of responses) and ecology (because it makes up 10% of responses and is too volatile), it's interesting to see that people who selected biology didn't select predictive or statistical modeling as much. I don't have much of an explanation for that. On the other hand, people who chose soc/poli sci and health did seem to select predictive and statistical modeling at a higher rate than average. Those fields I can see models being very useful, such as with elections or with predicting chances of diseases. Looking at the neural network row, it seems as though people who chose biology, neuroscience and software development are interested in neural networks slightly more than average. It is possible that those fields are better-suited to utilize neural networks. Looking at the image analysis row, it seems that biology and neuroscience selectors also are interested in image analysis AND text analysis. This (to me) is plausible since I can see those fields utilizing image recognition for stuff like cells or human bodies more often than not. Text analysis too since stuff those fields may have a lot of text data that needs to be converted. 

# Extra Ideas:
- Could use the same logic of the proportion deviation, but instead, compare all the responses that selected the domain compared to all the responses that DIDN'T select that same domain. Then you can have 2 groups that you can compare against. 
- Could try to create like a logistic regression model to predict whether a person marked a data science area as interesting to them using the domains as an input. Have one logistic regression model for each individual data science area

# Quick Summary of Work (10/13)
- Loaded in data and modified data to represent with many columns where each column represents whether the respondent marked that they were interested in that domain or data science area.
- Currently not handling write-in data through "Other" since I'm not sure the best way to handle this. 
- Created a frequency table of how many respondents marked an interest in a certain domain/subject combination. This is saved in the variable `domain_area_count_table`
- Realizing that 1 person doesn't necessarily equal 1 response, counts become not very comparable between domains since the number of people who chose each domain isn't equal. Hence, proportions seem better.
- Created a heatmap of the domain/area combinations.
- Note that chi-square tests probably won't work since each respondent technically can fall into multiple categories (see how the sum of the counts table adds up to 1396, and not 49 for the 49 responses)


# 10/15 Work
```{r Heatmap of Differences in Selections between People who Chose a Field and People who Didn't}
processed_data <- read_csv("../data/cleaned_combined_data.csv") %>% select(-(prog.comf:stat.comf), -("PSTAT 115": other_dept))

processed_data_long <- processed_data %>% pivot_longer(cols = envi_sci:software_dev, names_to = "domain", values_to = "selected") %>% select(response_id, domain, selected, image_analysis:algorithms)

props_by_selected_domain <- processed_data_long %>% group_by(domain, selected) %>% summarize(count = n(), across("image_analysis":"algorithms", mean))
props_by_selected_domain <- props_by_selected_domain %>% ungroup()
prop_by_domain_long <- props_by_selected_domain %>% pivot_longer(cols = "image_analysis":"algorithms", names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% select(count, domain, selected, area, proportion) %>% arrange(domain)


area_prop_diff_by_domain <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:8){
  data = props_by_selected_domain[c(2*i - 1, 2*i),]
  data = data %>% transmute(across(image_analysis:algorithms, diff)) %>% slice(1)
  area_prop_diff_by_domain <- rbind(area_prop_diff_by_domain, data)
}
area_prop_diff_by_domain <- area_prop_diff_by_domain %>% pivot_longer(cols = image_analysis:algorithms, names_to = "area", values_to = "prop_diff")
area_prop_diff_by_domain$domain <- factor(area_prop_diff_by_domain$domain, levels = domains_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(domain))
area_prop_diff_by_domain$area <- factor(area_prop_diff_by_domain$area, levels = areas_of_interest %>% arrange(count) %>% pull(area))

# Between people who expressed interest in a domain and those who didn't, each number shows the difference between the proportions in the two groups that also expressed interest in that data science area
area_prop_diff_by_domain %>% arrange(prop_diff) %>% filter(!(domain %in% c("ecology", "tech"))) %>% head(10)

```
### Biggest differences in proportions for interest in an area based on whether they are interested in a domain or not.
```{r Main Plot}
prop_diff_plot <- ggplot(data = area_prop_diff_by_domain, mapping = aes(x = domain, y = area, fill = prop_diff)) + 
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(prop_diff, 2)), col = "white") +
  labs(x = "Domain", y = "Area", title = "Comparing Proportion Differences of Area Preferences Based on Domain Preferences") +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 9))

prop_diff_plot
```
# Methodology
Within each domain, I stratify the data into 2 groups: people who expressed interest in a domain and those who didn't express interest in the domain. Within those groups, I calculate the proportion of people who also expressed interest in pursuing a specific area of data science. The number in each cell represents the difference in the proportions between the people interested in the domain versus those who aren't interested. 

For example: the 0.37 in the cell for `software_dev` and `data_engineering` means that the proportion of people interested in data engineering is 37 percentage points higher in the group interested in software development compared to the group not interested in software development 

I am wary of making conclusions in ecology and tech since those had very unbalanced groups of people who are interested/not interested in those domains.

# Notable Results:
- When comparing the differences in people interested in software development and those that are not interested, the people interested in software development seemed to have a higher proportion of interest in software integration, image analysis, data engineering, and neural networks compared to those who did not express interest in software development (at least 20 percentage points more!)

- The respondents interested in neuroscience were also more interested in image analysis compared to those not interested in neuroscience (38 percentage points more). Similar behavior was seen between those interested in health/biology compared to those who weren't interested. (Makes sense since imaging can be a significant part of those fields)

- Respondents interested in biology seemed to express less interest in statistical modeling compared to those not interested in biology. (32 percentage points lower) I don't have an explanation for this.
- The proportion of respondents interested in time series is 27 percentage points higher among those interested in environmental science compared to those that are not. (Maybe environmental science likes to look at long term trends which includes time series data)
- The proportion of respondents interested in statistical modeling is 31 percentage points higher in respondents interested in social and political science compared to those who are not. (Potentially may be because social and political science may use a lot of models to predict behavior or stuff like elections). Similar behavior was seen for predictive modeling and time series.

```{r}
interesting_result_1 <- props_by_selected_domain %>% filter(domain == "software_dev") %>% select(domain, selected, software_integration, image_analysis, data_engineering, neural_networks) %>% pivot_longer(cols = software_integration:neural_networks, names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = selected, values_from = proportion)

interesting_result_2 <- props_by_selected_domain %>% filter(domain %in% c("neurosci", "biology", "health")) %>% select(domain, selected, image_analysis) %>% pivot_longer(cols = image_analysis, names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = selected, values_from = proportion)

interesting_result_3 <- props_by_selected_domain %>% filter(domain == "biology") %>% select(domain, selected, statistical_modeling) %>% pivot_longer(cols = statistical_modeling, names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = selected, values_from = proportion)

interesting_result_4 <- props_by_selected_domain %>% filter(domain == "envi_sci") %>% select(domain, selected, time_series) %>% pivot_longer(cols = time_series, names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = selected, values_from = proportion)

interesting_result_5 <- props_by_selected_domain %>% filter(domain == "soc_poli_sci") %>% select(domain, selected, statistical_modeling, predictive_modeling, time_series) %>% pivot_longer(cols = c("statistical_modeling", "predictive_modeling", "time_series"), names_to = "area", values_to = "proportion") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = selected, values_from = proportion)

interesting_results <- rbind(interesting_result_1, interesting_result_2, interesting_result_3, interesting_result_4, interesting_result_5)
colnames(interesting_results) <- c("Domain", "Data Science Area", "Not Interested Prop.", "Interested Prop.") 
interesting_results %>% arrange("Domain")
```

```{r}
save(interesting_results, prop_diff_plot, area_int_strat_domain_plot, file = "question_1_results.rda")
```
